summary: In Greek mythology, Marsyas was a Phrygian satyr (or silenus) famed for the aulos. He took up the double pipes Athena had cast away, challenged Apollo to a musical contest, and when he lost was flayed alive near Celaenae; tears for him became the river Marsyas. Literary sources stress hubris and divine justice; Romans also cast him as a symbol of free speech in the Forum.

sections.heading: Family and the aulos
paragraphs: When a genealogy is given, Marsyas is son of Hyagnis, or of Oeagrus, or of Olympus — the last also named as his pupil or beloved. Melanippides and later tradition hold that Athena invented the aulos, saw her puffed cheeks in a mirror, threw the instrument away, and cursed whoever took it up. Marsyas found the pipes and mastered them; Pausanias saw Myron's sculptural group of Athena striking the silenus for picking them up, set before the Parthenon.

sections.heading: Contest with Apollo
paragraphs: Marsyas challenged Apollo; the Muses or Nysean nymphs judged, and the winner might treat the loser as he wished. Versions differ: Hyginus has Apollo win by playing the lyre upside-down, a feat impossible on the flute; Diodorus has Apollo add his voice to the lyre and argue that Marsyas's blowing was comparable. The satyr was flayed in a cave near Celaenae; Apollo nailed the skin to a pine by Lake Aulocrene. Ovid dwells on the tears of fauns, satyrs, and nymphs that formed the river Marsyas; Herodotus says the flayed skin was still shown at Celaenae.

Hyginus also brings King Midas into a related judging scene on Tmolus, where Midas prefers Marsyas and receives ass's ears from Apollo. Apollodorus names Marsyas son of Olympus and briefly records the challenge, hanging, and flaying.

sections.heading: Wise satyr and Roman liberty
paragraphs: Diodorus praises Marsyas for intelligence and self-control; Plato's Alcibiades likens Socrates to him. At Rome a statue of Marsyas near the comitium stood for centuries as an indicium libertatis — a mark of free speech associated with the plebs and Liber. The gens Marcia claimed descent from him; under Augustus the figure could read as oppositional. Later art (Titian, Ribera, and many others) made the flaying a set piece of Apollonian versus Dionysian struggle. This atlas node is the Phrygian satyr (marsyas-phrygia), not the river alone or Italian eponymic extensions.
